options: A reaction that absorbs energy from its surroundings
A reaction that releases energy to its surroundings
A reaction with no energy change
A reaction that only happens in fire
questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction absorbs energy — endo (in) + therm (heat), so energy flows inward.
questions.misconception: Releasing energy is the exothermic reaction's job — the endothermic reaction is specifically the one that ABSORBS energy from outside.

questions.prompt: What happens to the surroundings when an endothermic reaction runs?
options: They cool down — heat is pulled out of them
questions.explanation: An endothermic reaction pulls heat out of its surroundings, so the surroundings get colder — like a cold pack.
questions.misconception: It is the EXOTHERMIC reaction that warms things up — endothermic pulls heat out and leaves the surroundings colder.

questions.prompt: Why does an endothermic reaction absorb energy?
options: The products hold more energy than the reactants — the extra is pulled in
The reactants hold more energy than the products
Energy is destroyed during the reaction
questions.explanation: In an endothermic reaction the products are higher-energy, so the extra energy must be absorbed from the surroundings.
questions.misconception: Energy is never destroyed and atoms never appear — the absorption happens because the products need more energy than the reactants had.

questions.prompt: Which of these is an endothermic reaction?
options: A cold pack turning freezing when cracked
A log burning in a fire
questions.explanation: A cold pack absorbing heat and turning cold is a classic endothermic reaction — it pulls energy IN from its surroundings.
questions.misconception: Hand warmers, fires, and body warmth all give energy OUT — those are exothermic. The cold pack takes energy in, which is endothermic.
